chunks.content: Introduction Medial meniscus extrusion (MME) is defined as the displacement of the medial meniscus beyond the outer margin of the medial tibial plateau, shown in . While a small degree of extrusion can be physiologic under an axial load, a displacement of greater than 3 mm as measured on non-weightbearing MRI is considered pathological. , MME has mainly been considered a consequence of a medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT), as extrusion signified that the circumferential fibers were biomechanically inactive. In a healthy knee, the circumferential fibers convert axial forces into circumferential tensile stresses to distribute load across the tibial plateau and shield the underlying articular cartilage from excessive peak contact pressures. In a MMPRT, the damaged posterior meniscal root is unable to generate hoop stress, rendering it similar to a “functional total meniscectomy,” leaving the articular cartilage exposed to peak contact pressures. , The paradox of this pathology is that MME has been reported prior to a MMPRT, persisting or possibly worsening after a successful anatomic MMPRT repair, or in cases of early cartilage degeneration and osteophyte formation without root disruption , , Thus, MME may not be merely a sign of injury, but a dynamic process rooted in the failure of the entire knee joint. MMPRTs and MME are now seen as an important independent risk factor for osteoarthritis (OA), and the clinical approach to knee joint preservation is evolving as the association between extrusion and meniscal health is further explored. This narrative review will discuss (1) the evolving understanding of meniscal extrusion pathophysiology, (2) current treatment options for MMPRT and MME, and (3) future areas of research need to be explored. In accordance with the Scale for the Assessment of narrative review articles principles for narrative reviews, we predefined the aim of the narrative review and conducted a structure search using PubMed/MEDLINE to find original articles published between January 2005 and December 2025. The search was based on but not limited to terms such as “meniscal extrusion,” “meniscus root tear,” “medial meniscus root repair,” “transtibial pull-out,” “suture anchor,” “centralization,” “meniscotibial ligament,” “medial meniscus MRI,” “meniscus weight-bearing/upright MRI,” “medial meniscus ultrasound,” “medial meniscus physical therapy,” “postoperative protocol,” “medial meniscus extrusion MCID,” and “biologic meniscal healing.” Of the qualifying articles, we included randomized control trials, prospective/retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, consensus statements/guidelines, and biomechanical investigations relevant to MME as these studies provide the most robust data. Studies excluded included those not in English, insufficient outcome data, or not relevant to MME/MMPRTs. The novelty of this narrative review is that it addresses the current evidence of MME and reframes the discussion from current knowledge to possible solutions for MME. Pathophysiology Current emerging data questions whether meniscal extrusion is the inciting event or the final consequence of a MMPRT. This shift in perspective comes from a 2020 case series by Krych et al. in which all patients reportedly demonstrated disruption of the meniscotibial ligament (MTL) and meniscal extrusion prior to the subsequent diagnosis of an MMPRT. This finding challenges the conventional view that MME is a consequence of a MMPRT, and suggests that failure of the secondary meniscal stabilizers may initiate a cascade that culminates to a MMPRT. Using this new frame for meniscus pathophysiology, Krych et al. offered a rationale for why root repair alone may be insufficient in controlling meniscus extrusion. In the same study, meniscal extrusion increased from 3.3 to 5.5 mm at the time the MMPRT was identified on MRI. This finding theorizes that stress on the MTL leads to a degenerative dysfunction in its ability to stabilize the meniscus. With the peripheral stabilizer compromised, the meniscus begins to displace radially. This extrusion concentrates biomechanical forces onto the posterior root attachment, which eventually fails under the overloading tension, resulting in a complete tear. This clinical finding is supported by a biomechanical study by Doan et al., which found that the creation of an isolated MTL tear resulted in significant meniscal extrusion. Extrusion further increased with a MMPRT, which in turn caused an increase in the medial compartment pressures. It should be noted that MTL tears did not initially alter medial compartment contact mechanics, a finding that seems contradictory to the association of MME and OA. This discrepancy may be explained by the circumferential fibers being still intact, allowing for the meniscus to maintain axial load distribution in a static testing environment. Doan et al. results were from a cadaveric study which do not account for dynamic forces, cyclic loading, and the progressive biologic degeneration seen in native knees. As a result, it was theorized that the primary role of the MTL is to act as a peripheral tether to keep the meniscus centered. Extrusion from MTL injury was theorized to a piece of a broader pathophysiologic process, with additional factors such as MMPRT and chronic tissue degeneration,

may be explained by the circumferential fibers being still intact, allowing for the meniscus to maintain axial load distribution in a static testing environment. Doan et al. results were from a cadaveric study which do not account for dynamic forces, cyclic loading, and the progressive biologic degeneration seen in native knees. As a result, it was theorized that the primary role of the MTL is to act as a peripheral tether to keep the meniscus centered. Extrusion from MTL injury was theorized to a piece of a broader pathophysiologic process, with additional factors such as MMPRT and chronic tissue degeneration, that cumulate to cause the contact pressure dependent osteoarthritic changes. Emerging evidence suggests that MME may continue to worsen even after successful MMPRT repair, supporting a cumulative degenerative theory of failure. Krych reported that despite a 98% meniscal healing rate on postoperative MRI, mean extrusion increased from 1.9 to 2.6 mm at roughly six months follow-up after a transtibial medial root repair. Within this study, a cohort of 10 patients had a postoperative MRI at a mean of 16 days, prior to weightbearing on the MMPRT repair. There was a reported increased extrusion of 0.36 mm within this short timeframe, but this value was not significant ( p = 0.23). Kawada et al. reported a significant progression (3.63–4.59 mm) of MME at one year postoperatively, even in patients with healed MMPRTs confirmed by second-look arthroscopy. With the highest level of evidence, Tollefson's randomized control trial reported that medial meniscal extrusion significantly increased in 96.2% of patients at six months postoperatively compared to their preoperative measurements. shows preoperative and postoperative measurements of MME giving a visual representation of persistent, postoperative extrusion. Regardless of the pathophysiologic sequence of extrusion and root tears, MME association with knee OA has been clearly defined. Using T2 mapping MRI, Hada et al. showed that MME was strongly associated with medial tibial osteophyte distance, in patients with early-stage OA without MMPRT. A meta-analysis by Fong et al. reported that patients with existing OA were 3.86 times more likely to have major MME (defined as > 3 mm) compared to patients without OA. Chung et al. 2021 conducted a long-term study with a minimum 10-year follow-up, reporting that an increase in postoperative MME of more than 0.7 mm following a root repair was a predictor for clinical failure, defined as an ultimate conversion to a total knee arthroplasty. This clinical evidence points to MME as a global degenerative pathology, calling for advancements in the surgical approaches aimed at treating MME and MMPRTs. Where are we with meniscal extrusion treatment The current standard of care for MMPRTs and MME is an anatomic transtibial pull-out technique, which involves passing sutures through the torn meniscal root and channeling them through bone tunnels drilled from the anterior aspect of the tibia to the medial meniscus posterior root's native attachment site. The sutures are tensioned and secured with a cortical button on the anterior aspect of the tibia. Studies have demonstrated that nonanatomic placement of the MMPRT repair, even off by a margin as small as 5 mm, fails to restore normal joint contact mechanics and is functionally equivalent to leaving the root tear untreated. However, even a perfectly anatomic root repair does not necessarily resolve the broader biomechanical issue of meniscal extrusion, which behaves somewhat independently of tunnel accuracy. The distinction becomes evident when reviewing postoperative outcomes. A meta-analysis by Perry et al. investigated outcomes following MMPRT repair and highlighted a distinct disconnect between patient symptoms and the underlying mechanical state of their knees. Despite persistent meniscus extrusion following repair, patient reported improved Lysholm, Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores and only 5.9% of patients had progression of OA, measured by the Kellgren-Lawrence scale. This proposes a critical question: how do surgeons balance the worsening radiographic data of extrusion with the successful clinical data of patient satisfaction? This disconnect has been addressed by commentary on a second-look arthroscopy study that reported a healed MMPRT repair that demonstrates laxity during arthroscopy is biomechanically nonfunctional and leads to the same osteoarthritic progression as a failed repair. Although an intact meniscus initially protects the articular cartilage and provides pain relief, tissue laxity allows for further extrusion over time. A cadaveric study by Steineman et al. stated that repairs are subject to loosening under cyclic loading simulating postoperative rehabilitation. The extrusion in this study was due to the enlargement of the suture holes in the meniscus. Repetitive stress and friction during cyclic testing allowed the sutures to effectively saw into the meniscal tissue. It is important to note that no specimens in this study experienced failure of the MMPRT repair. As extrusion worsens, joint mechanics further deteriorate, contributing to the progression of OA. , Many experts believe that the phenomenon

MME has been recognized as biomechanically important, but it remains uncertain whether radiographic improvements should outweigh patients reported outcomes as a predictor of joint preservation. In practice, postoperative decision making should balance radiographic extrusion with positive patient outcomes, with caution against overtreating isolated radiographic extrusion in a clinically improving patient. Long-term studies examining patient outcomes, extrusion trajectories, and OA progression are needed to determine when MME should be prioritized as a target of clinical management. With the transtibial pull-out technique coming under question, alternative techniques, such as suture anchor techniques, have gained interest as biomechanical data and early clinical data appear promising. Recent biomechanical studies have shown that suture anchor repairs may exhibit less displacement under cyclic loading, better contact mechanics and compartment pressures, and improved healing on post-operative MRI. , Rebuttal against this innovation states that outcomes are highly dependent on suture construct design and deployment within a limited posterior space, implant prominence within the articular space, and that most proposed gain is related to biomechanical data with limit clinic data showing minimal to no improvement in patient reported outcomes. – Even with disadvantages described as greater displacement from meniscus-suture interface and morbidity of tunnel drilling, advantages such as reproducibility, diminished articular footprint, ability to target the native footprint for anatomic fixation, robust cortical fixation, and biological healing potential given marrow stimulation are reasons why the transtibial repairs has remained the standard of care. , Given the growing evidence that a transtibial MMPRT repair is not sufficient by itself to preserve the articular cartilage of the knee joint, several techniques have been developed to augment the repair. A meniscal centralization suture, also referred to as a peripheral stabilization suture, is a technique that secures the extruded meniscus back to the tibial plateau during root repair surgery. This highlights the function of the MTL as a secondary peripheral stabilizer. A centralization suture involves the placement of one or more all-suture anchors at the periphery of the tibial plateau. Sutures from these anchors are passed through the meniscus and tensioned to reduce the extruded meniscus to an anatomic position. Centralization was originally described for the lateral meniscus, but has since been successfully adapted as a possible augment to address MME. There are two primary approaches of centralization sutures: posteromedial anchoring and posteromedial tibial pullout technique. Posteromedial anchoring involves mobilizing the MTLs and then placing one to three knotless all-inside suture anchors in the rim of the tibial plateau. An all-inside meniscus repair device is used to place vertical mattress sutures through the outer rim of the extruded meniscus, through the capsule and MTL which tethers the repair stitch to the MTL without piercing the meniscus. The theoretical advantage of securing the MTL rather than suturing the meniscus body is that native anteroposterior motion of the meniscus in flexion and extension is maintained without potentially iatrogenically over-constraining the meniscus. Also, by avoiding meniscal body perforation, circumferential fibers are not disrupted, preserving a native environment for optimal hoop stress biomechanics. When tensioning the sutures, the meniscus is pulled back to its native position within the margin of the tibial plateau, reducing extrusion and centralizing it on the articular surface. , , In the posteromedial tibial pullout technique, sutures are passed through the posteromedial corner of the meniscus, before exiting through a tibial tunnel as shown in . illustrates literature that states there are techniques where the same transtibial tunnel as the MMPRT repair can be used, or a new tunnel can be created 15 mm medial to the root insertion, or at the midpoint between the posterior root attachment and the posterior border of the MCL. Regardless, the sutures are secured to the anteromedial tibial surface. A systematic review found that the posteromedial anchoring technique demonstrated a significant reduction in medial meniscal extrusion (mean difference range of −1.2 to −0.2 mm) within studies when comparing preoperative-to-postoperative changes in extrusion data. Posteromedial anchoring also showed more consistent improvements in extrusion compared to posteromedial transtibial pullout repair and isolated MMPRT repairs when indirectly compared with other studies. The ideal number and location of tibial anchors for centralization sutures have yet to be determined. One biomechanical study using porcine tissue reported that three sutures significantly reduced extrusion compared to two sutures. These sutures were placed 10 mm anterior to the posterior border of the medial collateral ligament. A separate porcine study reported that a suture placed at the apex of the posterior horn was most effective at reducing extrusion. In another porcine model conducted by Boksh et al., they reported that using two suture tapes reduced extrusion and improved joint mechanics compared to suture anchors. Daney et al. investigated the location of a centralization suture placed at the midpoint between the root attachment and the posterior border of the MCL. They reported no significant biomechanical differences found between the anatomic MMPRT repair and anatomic MMPRT repair with centralization state; however, the centralization suture did help reduce MME and contact mechanics in the nonanatomic repair model, which simulated a chronically extruded meniscus. Lastly, there is an ongoing debate regarding the most durable suture configuration for a MMPRT repair. Biomechanical studies have compared various constructs, including the modified Mason-Allen, two simple stitches, locking-loop stitches, and vertical mattress sutures, to evaluate which suture pattern offers the highest strength with minimal MME. , While the data is mixed on which provides the best results, optimizing suture materials, configurations, and fixation methods are needed to minimize MMPRT repair loosening as simulated rehabilitation studies show that loosening is unrecoverable with addition rehabilitation. , , Overall, the clinical outcomes suggest that a MMPRT repair with a centralization suture offers promising results. A case series with a mean follow-up of two years reported improvement in patient-reported outcomes including the Visual Analog Scale, KOOS jr., and the IKDC, indicating improvements in pain, function, and overall satisfaction. Three patients out of 25 obtained an MRI around five months postoperative: two for acute pain and one for research purposes. This provided radiographic evidence that supported centralization can improve MME and patient outcome scores. The three patients showed an average extrusion of 1.6 mm postoperatively compared to 3.3 mm preoperatively. There was no evidence of degenerative changes on postoperative radiographs of 23 out of 25 of the patients. None of the patients required revision meniscus surgery or TKA conversion within the two years follow-up timeframe. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that meniscal centralization sutures significantly reduced MME ( p < 0.00001) and restored MME to levels similar to the native knee from 0 to 90 degrees of flexion. Tibiofemoral contact pressure was reduced (3.2–5.0 times closer to the native biomechanics compared to MMPRT) and load sharing contact area was improved following a centralization suture. The clinical data reveal improved KOOS, Lysholm, and IKDC scores. Lastly centralization sutures had few complications with preserved ROM, joint space, and varus deformity with medial compartment disease. , Tollefson et al. conducted a randomized control trial with 26 patients that found the addition of a centralization suture to MMPRT repair resulted in significantly decreased postoperative extrusion at six months postoperatively compared to MMPRT repair alone. While the augmentation did not completely prevent extrusion, it reduced the progression of MME by over 50%. This study included patients with high BMI and varus malalignment, excluding extreme malignment at the surgeon's discretion, which are known risk factors for increasing medial compartment pressures promoting postoperative extrusion. In patients with residual varus, MMPRT repair with centralization may limit postoperative extrusion progression, but it may not eliminate it because the underlying coronal plane imbalance continues to bias the meniscus toward extrusion. Therefore, individual patient risk factors should be considered when interpreting extrusion outcomes after centralization. The authors attempted to protect the MMPRT repair and centralization suture by using an unloading bracing postoperatively to decrease medial compartment forces and limit MME in patients with varus deformity. To summarize, centralization sutures has been shown to reduce extrusion, improve contact mechanics and functional outcomes, preserve knee range of motion, and play a role in joint space preservation in early stages

Tollefson et al. hypothesized that continued extrusion may be related to poor quality of the meniscal tissue itself. Increased T2 values on high powered MRIs may be signs of increased meniscus volume, which could be a result of collagen matrix disorganization. It's plausible that this degenerative swollen tissue lacks the ability to resist extrusion, even after re-anchoring the root. recaps the key findings within this section. How can we solve meniscus extrusion Given the fact that patients report significant clinical improvement despite worsened extrusion after MMPRT, we must define what a successful MMPRT repair is. , The first step in doing so is standardizing imaging and the measurement of extrusion so the data may be conglomerated and analyzed. MRI is the current gold standard for identifying and measuring meniscus extrusion, with more than 95% of members of the Meniscus International Network (MenIN) favoring MRI as their primary imaging modality. , , However, a systematic review by Farivar et al. highlighted significant heterogeneity in the literature regarding how extrusion is classified. To classify as pathologic or physiologic, MME is measured using a coronal MRI scan from a medial structure to the peripheral border of the extruded meniscus. The review identified primary medial coronal landmarks used for measurement: the MCL (38%, most common), the midpoint of the anterior-posterior length of the medial meniscus (23% of studies), and the middle of the medial femoral condyle (19%). The pathologic threshold of >3 mm of MME is not universally agreed upon as some experts prefer a threshold of 4 mm. Svensson et al. found that a general population had an average of 2.7 mm of extrusion in knees without radiographic signs of OA. This meant that using 3 mm as “pathologic” for extrusion may be over labeling knees as degenerative without clinical or radiographic evidence. By raising the threshold to 4 mm, the sensitivity remained acceptable while specificity improved, resulting in a better overall ability to distinguish knees with degenerative changes from those without. , This lack of consensus in measurement and pathologic classification complicates direct comparison between studies. A growing body of evidence suggests that classifying MME by millimeters measured on an MRI may be an oversimplification. Extrusion varies with position and weight-bearing status, therefore, static imaging may not fully capture the dynamic behavior of the meniscus. Unloaded knees that were deemed “healthy” showed extrusion ranges from 0.7 to 1.1 mm. – Under an axial load, a “healthy” knee extrudes an additional 0.8–1.2 mm compared to baseline extrusion. – In pathologic states, such as MMPRT or mucoid degeneration, baseline and loaded states often report a higher values. – In Daney et al., they reported no difference in extrusion in every repair state (anatomic/nonanatomic, with or without centralization) in a unloaded knee in full extension, suggesting that axial stress and higher degrees of flexion may be required to evaluate MME. This was further supported in their study when maximal amount of meniscal extrusion was observed when the knee was loaded at 90 degrees of flexion. Patient-specific factors must be accounted for as well, as higher patient BMI has been shown to significantly increase the difference of extrusion on weightbearing ultrasound compared to supine imaging. Lastly, there is a phenomenon known as the “dead meniscus sign” which may be seen on ultrasound where the meniscus is maximally extruded and dynamic extrusion may fail to occur with weightbearing. Given these considerations, alternative imaging modalities and combined imaging may be better suited to identify extrusion due to the meniscus's dynamic nature. Notably a dynamic ultrasound study performed while walking found that MME was greater in osteoarthritic knees than in healthy controls, and in dynamic images compared to static weightbearing images. , Ultrasound offers excellent sensitivity (>90%) and specificity (>70%) for detecting meniscal extrusion and its dynamic cost-effective nature makes it a promising screening tool. Ultrasound can be followed by MRI for confirmation of extrusion, as well as to identify concomitant pathologies such as MMPRT or chondral lesions. CT scan may also be an option

Ultrasound can be followed by MRI for confirmation of extrusion, as well as to identify concomitant pathologies such as MMPRT or chondral lesions. CT scan may also be an option when MRI is not available. In addition to standardizing imaging modalities and measurement techniques, we must determine the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for extrusion reduction in order to define a successful MMPRT repair. The MCID is the smallest change in a specific patient-reported outcome that a patient perceives as beneficial. Although hypothetical, establishing a MCID would help determine how much reduction is necessary to produce meaningful improvements for patients and could help guide surgeons in selecting interventions most likely to yield clinical benefits. It may also help explain why patients feel clinical benefit despite persistent extrusion if they have achieved the MCID. In regard to patients, the clinical evidence strongly suggests a case-by-case approach to managing MME and MMPRT repair. To be set up for success, clear patient indications and contraindications must be defined. Patients with the best prognosis typically present with minimal pre-existing OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade I-II) and minimal varus alignment. , A MMPRT repair with a centralization suture is most effective with minimizing meniscus extrusion when the articular cartilage and overall joint environment are relatively preserved. , The most significant negative predictor for long-term success is a preoperative mechanical varus alignment greater than 5 degrees as a significant long-term risk factor for conversion to total knee arthroplasty. In such cases, addressing the MMPRT without correcting the underlying malalignment may be insufficient to stop degenerative extrusion. Patients with greater than 5 degrees of varus have been excluded from centralization suture studies as academic opinions often consider a high tibial osteotomy to correct the malalignment, unloading the medial compartment, limiting chronic degeneration in younger patients. , Other treatments, such as the use of medial unloader braces in these often older patients with MMPRTs, has also been proposed to protect a MMPRT repair in patients with varus alignment. In these cases, the braces are used preoperatively to allow patients to get used to wearing the medial unloader brace and then used postoperatively starting with weight bearing at 6 weeks and worn for all weight bearing activities until at least four months postoperatively. Additionally, a higher BMI is an established risk factor for the development of MMPRTs as it places increased mechanical stress on the post-surgical repair construct, contributing to poorer outcomes. , Lastly, delaying surgical intervention may have a negative impact on outcomes as well. A 2024 study by Krych et al. found that a longer duration of nonoperative treatment correlated with higher postoperative pain levels, with optimal surgical timeline within 13 weeks of symptom onset. Beyond patient selection, several modifiable factors play a crucial role in the ultimate structural and clinical success of the repair. A 2023 study by Kawada et al. identified a direct link between quadriceps function and the structural stability of the repair. The researchers found that greater postoperative quadriceps strength was significantly correlated with less progression of medial meniscal extrusion and better KOOS scores. This is clinically significant as it can be objectively targeted as a modifiable risk factor in physical therapy. Rehabilitation protocols can be highly varied and lack standardization, especially when factoring in new techniques such as a centralization suture. , This is particularly concerning given the biomechanical evidence showing that early or improper weightbearing can cause unrecoverable loosening and failure of the repair construct. , A postoperative protocol, as described by Monson et al., states nonweightbearing for 6 weeks, with protected range of motion less than 90 degrees for 2 weeks, and then graduated weightbearing and range of motion increases as the patient progresses. This approach allows for biological healing of the MMPRT, limiting postoperative stiffness, and protecting the repair construct. Addressing the poor intrinsic healing capacity of the meniscus is a critical frontier. Biological augmentation strategies, such as platelet-rich plasma, fibrin clots, marrow venting, and degradable implants aim to create a more favorable environment for tissue healing and regeneration. While there are biological theories behind these procedures, these modalities have failed to translate into high-level clinical evidence, with human trials yielding mixed results. , Tissue level investigational research will be needed to address the gaps of biologic meniscal healing. Despite increasing interest in meniscus extrusion, high-quality evidence to guide repair strategies remains limited, specifically randomized controlled trials. The Tollefson et al.

While there are biological theories behind these procedures, these modalities have failed to translate into high-level clinical evidence, with human trials yielding mixed results. , Tissue level investigational research will be needed to address the gaps of biologic meniscal healing. Despite increasing interest in meniscus extrusion, high-quality evidence to guide repair strategies remains limited, specifically randomized controlled trials. The Tollefson et al. randomized control trial provided critical data comparing root repair with and without a centralization suture showed that centralization significantly diminishes the postoperative increase in extrusion. More studies like this are required to continue to advance the field. As seen with Daney et al., cadaveric studies at time zero may report similar findings to standard MMPRT repair and MMPRT repair plus a centralization suture, but may not totally represent how the repair acts in clinical settings after withstanding thousands of loading cycles during postoperative rehabilitation. The primary goal of a root repair is preventing long-term OA, yet most studies are limited to short-term follow-up roughly around two years of data. , Future studies should attempt to elucidate the optimal meniscus extrusion method and to investigate long-term durability of such repairs. , Lastly, heterogeneity in extrusion measurement methods complicates cross-study comparisons. To overcome this, establishment of large, standardized, multi-center patient registries are essential to track outcomes over 5- to 10-year periods. , Future studies should also evaluate outcomes of combined root repair, centralization sutures, and MTL techniques as no study to date has investigated a comprehensive, multi-tissue stabilization strategy that addresses the meniscus root, the MTL, and the meniscus capsule. As a narrative review, this article is limited by potential selection bias and decreased reproducibility due to no strictly predefined protocol. The currently available evidence regarding centralization techniques, biomechanical rationale, and clinical outcomes originates from a limited number of high-volume research groups. While this reflects expertise in the field, it introduces the possibility of confirmation or publication bias. Conclusions The understanding of meniscus extrusion has evolved drastically over the past decade. Once viewed as a consequence of MMPRTs, meniscus extrusion is now recognized as an early step in the degenerative process. Evidence shows that a standard MMPRT repair can heal the posterior attachment but may be insufficient to correct the extrusion that can predispose to long-term joint failure. With evidence suggesting that a difference of less than 1 mm of postoperative extrusion may be the difference between a successful repair and progression towards a total knee arthroplasty, surgical augments to specifically address extrusion should be explored. Meniscus centralization sutures appear to be a promising technique with early clinical and radiographic data showing that this combined approach, standard transtibial MMPRT repair plus a centralization suture, could successfully reduce extrusion, improve patient-reported outcomes, and decrease the progression of OA at short-term follow-up. This combined approach may represent a shift in the management of MMPRT, from isolated repairs to comprehensive restoration.

documents.title: AAOS clinical practice guideline pediatric supracondylar humerus fracture

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Appropriate Use Criteria (AAOS AUC) provide evidence-based guidance for managing paediatric supracondylar humerus fractures, yet adherence to these guidelines varies widely in clinical practice. Previous studies have documented suboptimal concordance with the AUC, particularly for borderline cases, such as Gartland type II fractures. Most existing literature on AUC implementation is retrospective or simulation based, with limited prospective quality improvement data, especially from low- and middle-income countries. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This prospective three-cycle plan–do–study–act quality improvement project demonstrates that a phased, multifaceted intervention combining education, protocol development, visual reminders and individualised audit feedback can achieve a 25.8% absolute improvement in adherence to evidence-based guidelines for paediatric supracondylar humerus fractures. The study identifies key modifiable barriers to guideline adherence, including lack of awareness, absence of standardised protocols and variable surgeon preferences. Importantly, the study demonstrates successful implementation of the AAOS AUC in a resource-constrained tertiary care setting in a middle-income country, with sustained improvements maintained over a 7-month follow-up period. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This study provides a practical, replicable framework for implementing evidence-based guidelines in orthopaedic trauma care that can be adapted to diverse healthcare settings, including resource-limited environments. The findings suggest that sustained educational interventions with ongoing reinforcement and audit feedback are essential for long-term practice change, rather than one-time educational sessions alone. The study’s emphasis on low-cost interventions integrated into existing workflows offers a pragmatic approach for institutions seeking to improve guideline adherence without requiring substantial additional resources. Future research should focus on linking AUC adherence with patient outcomes and expanding similar quality improvement initiatives to other common paediatric fractures. Introduction Supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are the most common elbow injuries in children, accounting for up to 70% of paediatric elbow fractures and approximately 15% of all childhood fractures worldwide. These injuries typically occur between the ages of 5 and 7 years, most commonly following a fall on an outstretched hand. Despite their frequency, SCHF remains clinically significant due to the high risk of complications, including neurovascular injury, compartment syndrome, malunion and cubitus varus deformity. Management strategies for SCHF vary considerably across institutions and individual surgeons. While stable, non-displaced fractures (Gartland type I) are typically managed conservatively with immobilisation, displaced fractures (types II and III) often require reduction and percutaneous fixation. However, controversy persists regarding the optimal management of borderline cases, particularly Gartland type II fractures, where decisions between casting and surgical pinning are influenced by multiple factors, including fracture stability, swelling severity and neurovascular status. To address this variability and standardise care, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) developed appropriate use criteria (AUC) for paediatric SCHF management in 2014. The AUC synthesise available evidence and expert consensus into scenario-based recommendations, categorising treatment options as ‘Appropriate’, ‘May Be Appropriate’ or ‘Rarely Appropriate’ based on fracture type (Gartland classification), vascular status, neurological status, soft-tissue condition, associated injuries and swelling severity. Through a web-based tool, surgeons can rapidly match a patient’s clinical presentation to recommended treatment strategies, theoretically reducing unwarranted practice variation and improving outcomes. However, real-world validation and implementation of the AAOS AUC outside North America remains limited. Most available reports are retrospective or simulation based, and few prospective quality improvement studies have systematically evaluated interventions to improve AUC adherence. Moreover, there is scarce data from low- and middle-income countries, where variations in resources, training and healthcare infrastructure may affect guideline adoption and concordance. Prior to this project, our institution, a high-volume tertiary referral centre in Egypt receiving over 150 paediatric SCHF annually, had no standardised protocol for applying the AAOS AUC. An initial internal review suggested that management decisions were predominantly based on individual surgeon preference and training background rather than evidence-based guidelines, leading to potential overuse of ‘rarely appropriate’ treatments, particularly for Gartland type II fractures. This quality improvement project was, therefore, initiated with the primary aim of improving the proportion of paediatric SCHF cases managed ‘appropriately’ according to the AAOS AUC. We hypothesised that a multifaceted, phased intervention involving education, protocol implementation and system-level changes would lead to significant and sustained improvement in adherence to these evidence-based standards. Secondary aims included identifying the key barriers to AUC adherence and developing sustainable strategies to maintain improvement over time. Methods Study design and setting We conducted a prospective, three-cycle plan–do–study–act (PDSA) quality improvement project at the Emergency Hospital of Mansoura University, a tertiary referral centre in the Nile Delta region of Egypt. The hospital serves a catchment population of approximately 5 million and receives paediatric trauma referrals from multiple governorates. The project spanned from January 2021 to May 2023. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (2.0) guidelines. Methods Study design and setting We conducted a prospective, three-cycle plan–do–study–act (PDSA) quality improvement project at the Emergency Hospital of Mansoura University, a tertiary referral centre in the Nile Delta region of Egypt. The hospital serves a catchment population of approximately 5 million and receives paediatric trauma referrals from multiple governorates. The project spanned from January 2021 to May 2023. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (2.0) guidelines. Participants All children under the age of 18 years presenting to our institution with an acute (less than 14 days from injury) SCHF during the three audit periods were eligible for inclusion. Patients were excluded if they had pathological fractures, presented more than 14 days after injury (classified as neglected fractures), or had incomplete medical records that prevented accurate AUC assessment. PDSA cycles and interventions The project was structured around three distinct PDSA cycles, each building on the lessons learnt from the previous cycle. Cycle 1 served as a baseline assessment phase to quantify current practice patterns and identify barriers to guideline adherence, without implementing any interventions. Subsequent cycles (Cycles 2 and 3) incorporated the four components of the PDSA methodology with planned interventions, implementation, evaluation and adaptation based on findings. Cycle 1: baseline assessment (January 2021–June 2021) Plan The initial phase aimed to quantify the baseline adherence to the AAOS AUC for paediatric SCHF management at our institution. We planned to collect prospective data on all eligible patients over a 6-month period to establish current practice patterns and identify the primary areas of non-concordance with AUC recommendations. Do Data were prospectively collected for 58 consecutive patients meeting inclusion criteria. For each case, detailed clinical information was recorded, including fracture type (Gartland classification based on true lateral radiographs), vascular status (non-perfused, perfused but pulseless or perfused with palpable pulse), neurological status (median, radial and ulnar nerve integrity), soft-tissue envelope (closed vs open), swelling severity (typical vs severe) and associated injuries. The treating surgeon’s management plan was documented. A senior orthopaedic resident, not involved in the patient’s direct care, then independently entered each clinical scenario into the official AAOS AUC web-based tool to determine the appropriateness rating for the actual treatment provided. Study Analysis of the baseline data revealed that only 62.1% (36/58) of cases were managed ‘appropriately’ according to the AUC. The rate of ‘rarely appropriate’ management was 19.0% (11/58), with the highest non-concordance found in the management of Gartland type II fractures. Specifically, 65% of type IIa fractures were managed with casting alone, which the AUC rates as ‘rarely appropriate’ for unstable or significantly displaced type II fractures. Postcycle surveys and focus group discussions with the surgical team identified key barriers: 78% of surgeons were unfamiliar with the AAOS AUC web tool, there was no departmental consensus on type II fracture management and treatment decisions were based primarily on individual surgeon training and preference. Act Based on these findings, we planned a multimodal intervention aimed at increasing awareness of the AUC, providing clear guidance on evidence-based management and establishing a departmental protocol. Cycle 2: educational intervention and protocol implementation (September 2021–February 2022) Plan We hypothesised that a targeted educational programme combined with the introduction of a standardised departmental protocol would significantly increase the rate of ‘appropriate’ management. The intervention was designed and implemented between July and August 2021. Do The intervention consisted of two components. Educational Workshop (July 2021) : A mandatory 2-hour educational session was conducted for all orthopaedic residents and consultants. The workshop covered: (a) the evidence base for the AAOS AUC, including review of key studies; (b) live demonstration of the AUC web-based tool with case-based exercises; (c) discussion of common scenarios and areas of controversy, particularly type II fracture management and (d) distribution of pocket reference cards summarising AUC recommendations. Departmental Protocol Development (August 2021) : A multidisciplinary team, including senior consultants, residents and the quality improvement lead, developed a departmental protocol for SCHF management that explicitly integrated AUC recommendations. The protocol included a flowchart for type II fracture decision-making based on stability, displacement and swelling. Data were then prospectively collected for 62 patients in the 6 months following the intervention (September 2021–February 2022). Study The rate of ‘appropriate’ management increased to 75.8% (47/62), representing a 13.7% absolute improvement. The rate of ‘rarely appropriate’ cases decreased from 19.0% to 9.7% (6/62). For type IIa fractures, ‘rarely appropriate’ management decreased from 65% to 25%. However, analysis revealed persistent barriers: documentation of the AUC rating was inconsistent (completed in only 45% of cases), some senior surgeons expressed resistance to changing their established practices and the web-based tool was perceived as time-consuming in the emergency setting. Act To address these remaining barriers and ensure sustainability, we planned a comprehensive reinforcement

The rate of ‘rarely appropriate’ cases decreased from 19.0% to 9.7% (6/62). For type IIa fractures, ‘rarely appropriate’ management decreased from 65% to 25%. However, analysis revealed persistent barriers: documentation of the AUC rating was inconsistent (completed in only 45% of cases), some senior surgeons expressed resistance to changing their established practices and the web-based tool was perceived as time-consuming in the emergency setting. Act To address these remaining barriers and ensure sustainability, we planned a comprehensive reinforcement strategy, including refresher training and regular case discussions. Cycle 3: reinforcement education and sustained improvement (November 2022–May 2023) Plan We aimed to sustain and further improve AUC adherence through reinforcement education, regular case-based learning and visual reminders. The intervention was implemented between March and October 2022. Do The intervention included three components. Reinforcement Training Workshops (March–April 2022) : A series of three refresher workshops were conducted for all orthopaedic staff, focusing on challenging case scenarios, particularly Gartland type II fractures. Interactive case-based discussions were used to reinforce AUC principles. AUC training was incorporated into the mandatory orientation for new residents. Visual Reminders and Decision Aids (May 2022) : Large, laminated AUC flowcharts and decision aids were posted in the emergency department, operating theatre preparation area and orthopaedic ward. Pocket-sized quick reference cards were distributed to all clinicians and updated regularly. Local Departmental Presentations (August–September 2022) : Senior residents and consultants delivered presentations at departmental grand rounds showcasing successful cases managed according to AUC and discussing lessons learnt from non-concordant cases. Data were subsequently collected for 58 patients over a 7-month period (November 2022–May 2023). Study The rate of ‘appropriate’ management further increased to 87.9% (51/58), a 12.1% improvement from Cycle 2 and a total 25.8% improvement from baseline. The rate of ‘rarely appropriate’ cases fell to just 3.4% (2/58). For type IIa fractures, ‘rarely appropriate’ management decreased to 10%. The use of the AUC tool for decision-making was documented in over 95% of cases, indicating successful integration into routine practice. Postcycle surveys revealed high satisfaction with the reinforcement interventions, with 91% of surgeons reporting increased confidence in applying the AUC and 85% finding the weekly case discussions ‘very helpful’. Act The changes were adopted as standard departmental policy. Weekly case review meetings and visual reminders. AUC training was permanently incorporated into resident orientation, and the departmental protocol was updated to include mandatory AUC documentation for all SCHF cases. Measures and analysis The primary outcome measure was the proportion of paediatric SCHF cases managed ‘appropriately’ as defined by the AAOS AUC. Secondary outcomes included the following. The proportion of cases managed as ‘may be appropriate’. The proportion of cases managed as ‘rarely appropriate’. AUC tool utilisation rate (proportion of cases with documented AUC assessment). Appropriateness rates stratified by fracture type (Gartland I, IIa, IIb, III and flexion). Documented barriers to appropriate management Data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were summarised using means and standard deviations (or ranges where appropriate), while categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages. Given the quality improvement nature of this project and the sequential implementation of interventions, formal inferential statistical testing was not the primary focus. Instead, results from the three cycles were compared with assessing the impact of the interventions, and run charts were used to visualise changes in the primary outcome over time. All analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel 2019. The run chart displays monthly data points for the proportion of appropriate management throughout the study period, with the median line and intervention points marked to facilitate the interpretation of trends and sustainability of improvements. Results Patient demographics and clinical characteristics A total of 178 patients meeting the inclusion criteria were included across the three audit cycles: 58 in Cycle 1, 62 in Cycle 2 and 58 in Cycle 3. The demographic and clinical characteristics remained consistent across all three cycles, ensuring comparability of results. The mean age of the total cohort was 6.0±3.3 years (range 1–16 years), with 94 children (52.8%) aged 5 years or younger. There was a male predominance, with 120 males (67.4%) and 58 females (32.6%), consistent with the epidemiology of paediatric SCHF reported in the literature. Gartland type III extension fractures were the most common presentation, accounting for 109 cases (61.2%). Type I fractures were seen in 21 patients (11.8%), type IIa in 25 patients (14.0%), type IIb in 17 patients (9.6%) and flexion-type fractures in 6 patients (3.4%). The vast majority of patients presented with perfused hands and palpable distal pulses (168 patients, 94.4%). Eight patients (4.5%) had perfused hands without palpable pulses (‘pink pulseless hand’) and two patients (1.1%) presented with non-perfused hands requiring urgent intervention. No neurological deficits were documented at initial presentation

with the epidemiology of paediatric SCHF reported in the literature. Gartland type III extension fractures were the most common presentation, accounting for 109 cases (61.2%). Type I fractures were seen in 21 patients (11.8%), type IIa in 25 patients (14.0%), type IIb in 17 patients (9.6%) and flexion-type fractures in 6 patients (3.4%). The vast majority of patients presented with perfused hands and palpable distal pulses (168 patients, 94.4%). Eight patients (4.5%) had perfused hands without palpable pulses (‘pink pulseless hand’) and two patients (1.1%) presented with non-perfused hands requiring urgent intervention. No neurological deficits were documented at initial presentation in any patient. Nearly all fractures were closed (175 patients, 98.3%), with only three open fractures. Associated ipsilateral forearm or hand fractures were rare, occurring in nine patients (5.1%). Typical swelling was noted in 152 patients (85.4%), while severe swelling was present in 26 patients (14.6%). The detailed demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort are presented in . Primary outcome: appropriateness of management across cycles The primary outcome—the proportion of patients receiving ‘appropriate’ management according to the AAOS AUC—increased significantly across the three cycles. In Cycle 1 (baseline), 62.1% (36/58) of cases were managed appropriately. Following the educational intervention and protocol implementation in Cycle 2, this increased to 75.8% (47/62), representing a 13.7% absolute improvement. After the reinforcement training, visual reminders, case discussions and individualised feedback in Cycle 3, the rate of appropriate management reached 87.9% (51/58), a further 12.1% improvement and a total absolute improvement of 25.8% from baseline. Concurrently, the rate of ‘rarely appropriate’ management, which was the primary target for reduction, decreased from 19.0% (11/58) at baseline to 9.7% (6/62) in Cycle 2, and finally to 3.4% (2/58) in Cycle 3, representing an absolute reduction of 15.6%. The rate of ‘may be appropriate’ management also showed a steady decline, from 19.0% (11/58) in Cycle 1 to 14.5% (9/62) in Cycle 2, and to 8.6% (5/58) in Cycle 3. These results are summarised and illustrated in . Treatment modalities Closed reduction with percutaneous cross pinning was the most common treatment modality across all cycles, used in 133 patients (74.7%). Immobilisation without reduction was employed in 37 patients (20.8%), lateral pinning in 6 patients (3.4%) and open reduction with internal fixation in 2 patients (1.1%). Traction and external fixation were not used in any cases. The distribution of treatment modalities remained relatively stable across cycles, but the appropriateness of the chosen treatment for the specific fracture pattern and clinical scenario improved significantly. Barriers to appropriate management Systematic documentation and analysis of barriers to appropriate management revealed evolving challenges across the three cycles. Cycle 1 barriers: the primary barriers identified through postcycle surveys and focus group discussions were as follows. Lack of awareness of the AAOS AUC tool (78% of surgeons unfamiliar with the web-based tool). Absence of a standardised departmental protocol for type II fractures (100% of cases managed according to individual surgeon preference). Variable surgeon preferences based on training background and prior experience. No systematic documentation of appropriateness or decision-making rationale. Perception that AUC was developed for North American practice and might not apply to our setting. Cycle 2 barriers: despite the educational intervention, several barriers persisted. Incomplete uptake of the web-based tool (documented use in only 45% of cases). Time constraints in the emergency setting (average time to complete web tool: 3–5 min). Resistance from some senior surgeons to change established practices (documented in 23% of consultants). Lack of real-time decision support at the point of care. Inconsistent documentation of AUC assessment. Cycle 3 barriers: with sustained reinforcement interventions and regular audit feedback, most barriers were successfully addressed. Tool utilisation increased to 95% of cases through visual reminders and weekly case discussions. Surgeon engagement improved significantly with regular case-based learning. The remaining ‘rarely appropriate’ cases (3.4%) were primarily due to clinical judgement calls in borderline scenarios rather than lack of awareness. Two cases involved complex clinical scenarios with multiple comorbidities where the treating surgeon documented reasons for deviation from AUC recommendations. Discussion This three-cycle quality improvement project successfully demonstrates that a systematic, multifaceted approach can significantly improve adherence to the AAOS AUC for paediatric SCHF in a real-world clinical setting. By progressing from education and protocolisation to sustained reinforcement with visual reminders, case discussions and individualised feedback, we achieved a 25.8% absolute increase in ‘appropriate’ management and a corresponding 15.6% decrease in ‘rarely appropriate’ care. Our findings underscore the importance of moving beyond passive educational strategies to actively embedding evidence-based guidelines into routine practice through continuous reinforcement and audit feedback. Our findings underscore the importance of moving beyond passive educational strategies to actively embedding evidence-based guidelines into routine practice through continuous reinforcement and audit feedback. Comparison with existing literature The initial baseline of 62.1% appropriate care in our study is comparable with other single-centre studies conducted before targeted interventions. Brandt et al reported 68% concordance with AAOS AUC in a retrospective review of 156 patients at a paediatric level 1 trauma centre in the USA. Similarly, Douleh et al found 71% concordance in a simulation-based study. Our baseline is notably lower than these reports, possibly reflecting differences in baseline awareness of the AUC in different healthcare settings and the challenges of guideline implementation in resource-limited contexts. The main source of non-concordance in our study—the conservative management of Gartland type II fractures—is a well-documented area of clinical uncertainty and practice variation. The AAOS clinical practice guideline acknowledges that evidence for type II fracture management is limited, with most recommendations based on expert consensus rather than high-quality randomised trials. Our first intervention, combining education with a formal protocol, led to a significant 13.7% improvement, highlighting that the lack of awareness and absence of clear guidance were key initial barriers. This aligns with quality improvement literature emphasising the role of education as a foundational step in changing clinical practice. However, the substantial jump to 87.9% appropriate care was only achieved after implementing sustained reinforcement interventions: refresher training, visual reminders, regular case discussions and individualised audit feedback. This multifaceted approach addressed the persistent barriers of inconsistent documentation, resistance to change and lack of ongoing reinforcement. This finding is consistent with a growing body of evidence suggesting that sustained educational interventions combined with audit and feedback are among the most effective strategies for promoting guideline adherence and reducing practice variation. Ivers et al demonstrated in a Cochrane systematic review that audit and feedback can lead to significant improvements in professional practice, particularly when feedback is provided regularly and includes specific, actionable recommendations. Strengths and limitations Strengths of this study include its prospective design, relatively large cohort for a single-centre quality improvement project, systematic application of the AUC tool to all cases and the use of a rigorous PDSA methodology with iterative learning. The three-cycle approach allowed us to test and refine interventions progressively, identifying what worked and what did not. The sustained educational interventions and regular audit feedback represent sustainable, system-level changes that are likely to maintain improvements over time. Additionally, this is one of the first quality improvement studies to evaluate AAOS AUC implementation in a low- and middle-income country setting, providing valuable insights for similar contexts. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. As a single-centre study in a specific healthcare context, our findings may not be directly generalisable to all settings, particularly those with different educational resources, staffing models or case volumes. We did not collect data on clinical outcomes (such as the rates of malunion, neurovascular complications or need for reoperation), so we cannot definitively state that the increase in ‘appropriate’ care led to improved patient outcomes, although this is the implicit goal of the AUC. The Hawthorne effect may have influenced behaviour, as clinicians were aware they were a part of a quality improvement project, potentially leading to better performance than would occur in routine practice. The time gap between Cycle 2 and Cycle 3 (March–October 2022 for intervention implementation) means that some improvement might be attributable to maturation effects or secular trends rather than the specific interventions. Finally, we did not assess inter-rater reliability in AUC classification, although we used the official web-based tool that provides standardised ratings. Implications for practice Our findings have several important implications for clinical practice and quality improvement efforts. First, they demonstrate that the AAOS AUC can be successfully implemented in diverse healthcare settings, including low- and middle-income countries, with appropriate adaptation and support. Second, they highlight that education alone, while necessary, is insufficient for sustained practice change. Ongoing reinforcement through visual reminders, regular case discussions and audit feedback is crucial for embedding evidence-based practices into routine care. Third, individualised feedback to surgeons, comparing their performance with departmental averages, appears to be a powerful motivator for behaviour change, consistent with audit and feedback literature. For institutions seeking to implement similar quality improvement initiatives, our experience suggests a phased approach: (1) establish baseline performance and identify specific barriers through surveys and focus groups; (2) implement education and develop consensus protocols to address knowledge gaps; (3) provide sustained reinforcement through visual aids, regular case-based learning and departmental presentations; (4) implement individualised audit feedback to clinicians with regular reporting and (5) establish ongoing monitoring and case review processes to

For institutions seeking to implement similar quality improvement initiatives, our experience suggests a phased approach: (1) establish baseline performance and identify specific barriers through surveys and focus groups; (2) implement education and develop consensus protocols to address knowledge gaps; (3) provide sustained reinforcement through visual aids, regular case-based learning and departmental presentations; (4) implement individualised audit feedback to clinicians with regular reporting and (5) establish ongoing monitoring and case review processes to sustain improvements. Adaptation to local context is critical for successful implementation. Institutions must first ensure that clinicians have access to the AAOS AUC web-based decision tool (available at www.orthoguidelines.org/auc ) and are trained in its use, as this tool provides real-time guidance for clinical decision-making. In resource-constrained settings, we recommend prioritising low-cost interventions that integrate into the existing workflows, such as laminated pocket cards, visual flowcharts in clinical areas and incorporation of guideline training into routine educational activities rather than creating separate dedicated sessions. Leadership support for protected training time and establishment of formal governance structures with clearly defined roles enhance sustainability. Starting with small-scale pilot testing before broader implementation allows for iterative refinement based on local barriers and facilitators. Regular data collection with visual display methods (such as run charts) maintains team engagement and provides objective evidence of improvement. Future directions Based on our PDSA findings, future quality improvement efforts should focus on several areas. First, we plan to expand the educational interventions and visual decision aids to include other common paediatric fractures (such as forearm fractures and ankle fractures) where AAOS or other professional society guidelines exist. Second, we aim to link AUC adherence data with clinical outcomes to determine whether higher adherence rates are associated with improved patient outcomes, reduced complications or decreased healthcare costs. Third, we plan to conduct a multicentre implementation study to assess the generalisability of our approach to other institutions in Egypt and the broader Middle East and North Africa region. Finally, we will explore opportunities to develop institution-specific adaptations of the AUC that account for local resource availability while maintaining evidence-based principles. Conclusion This quality improvement project successfully implemented the AAOS AUC for paediatric SCHFs into routine clinical practice at a high-volume tertiary centre in Egypt. Through a structured, three-cycle PDSA approach, we demonstrated that combining education, departmental protocols, sustained reinforcement training and audit feedback can lead to significant and sustainable improvements in evidence-based care. The proportion of cases managed appropriately increased from 62.1% to 87.9%, while rarely appropriate management decreased from 19.0% to 3.4%. The key lessons from this project are that organisational factors—particularly lack of awareness, absence of standardised protocols and insufficient reinforcement mechanisms—represent the primary modifiable barriers to guideline adherence. Sustained educational interventions with visual reminders, regular case-based discussions and individualised audit feedback are powerful strategies for bridging the gap between evidence and practice. This approach is feasible and effective even in resource-limited settings, provided that there is institutional support, multidisciplinary collaboration and a commitment to iterative learning through PDSA methodology.

documents.title: AAOS clinical practice guideline pediatric diaphyseal femur fracture

chunks.content: Pediatric Supracondylar Humerus and Diaphyseal Femur Fractures: A Comparative Analysis of Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer and Google Gemini Recommendations Versus American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, including chat generative pretrained transformer (ChatGPT) and Google Gemini, have significantly increased access to medical information. However, in pediatric orthopaedics, no study has evaluated the accuracy of AI chatbots compared with evidence-based recommendations, including the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons clinical practice guidelines (AAOS CPGs). The aims of this study were to compare responses by ChatGPT-4.0, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Gemini with AAOS CPG recommendations on pediatric supracondylar humerus and diaphyseal femur fractures regarding accuracy, supplementary and incomplete response patterns, and readability. ChatGPT-4.0, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Gemini were prompted by questions created from 13 evidence-based recommendations (6 from the 2011 AAOS CPG on pediatric supracondylar humerus fractures; 7 from the 2020 AAOS CPG on pediatric diaphyseal femur fractures). Responses were anonymized and independently evaluated by 2 pediatric orthopaedic attending surgeons. Supplementary responses were, in addition, evaluated on whether no, some, or many modifications were necessary. Readability metrics (response length, Flesch-Kincaid reading level, Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning Fog Index) were compared. Cohen Kappa interrater reliability (κ) was calculated. χ 2 analyses and single-factor analysis of variance were utilized to compare categorical and continuous variables, respectively. Statistical significance was set with P <0.05. ChatGPT-4.0, ChatGPT-3.5, and Google Gemini were accurate in 11/13, 9/13, and 11/13, supplementary in 13/13, 11/13, and 13/13, and incomplete in 3/13, 4/13, and 4/13 recommendations, respectively. Of 37 supplementary responses, 17 (45.9%), 19 (51.4%), and 1 (2.7%) required no, some, and many modifications, respectively. There were no significant differences in accuracy ( P = 0.533), supplementary responses ( P = 0.121), necessary modifications ( P = 0.580), and incomplete responses ( P = 0.881). Overall κ was moderate at 0.55. ChatGPT-3.5 provided shorter responses ( P = 0.002), but Google Gemini was more readable in terms of Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level ( P = 0.002), Flesch Reading Ease ( P < 0.001), and Gunning Fog Index ( P = 0.021). While AI chatbots provided responses with reasonable accuracy, most supplemental information required modification and had complex readability. Improvements are necessary before AI chatbots can be reliably used for patient education. Level IV.
